title: Πίθοι
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Priam’s plea has moved Achilles to tears, and the two men weep together, one for Hector, the other for his father and for Patroclus. Achilles raises the old man, pities him, and asks how he dared come alone to the man who killed his sons. He tells Priam of the two jars on the floor of Zeus, one of evils and one of good gifts, and of how Peleus was blessed and then cursed with a single doomed son, far from home. Priam cannot sit while Hector lies unburied and asks to be given him at once. Achilles answers sharply, but says he already means to release the body, for his mother has brought word from Zeus, and he warns Priam not to provoke him further. The old man obeys. The attendants unyoke the wagon and bring in the ransom, leaving two cloaks and a tunic; Achilles has the maids wash and anoint the body out of Priam’s sight, lest his grief provoke Achilles to kill him. Achilles himself lifts Hector onto the wagon and tells Patroclus not to be angry that he gave Hector back.

sentences.t: ὣς φάτο, τῷ δ’ ἄρα πατρὸς ὑφ’ ἵμερον ὦρσε γόοιο·
sentences.tr: hōs phato, tōi d’ ara patros hyph’ himeron ōrse gooio·
sentences.l: So he spoke, and in him then for his father it aroused a longing of lament.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and it stirred in him a longing to weep for his father.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο ‘so he spoke’ closes Priam’s speech from the previous part. The one who is moved is Achilles (τῷ, ‘in him’), and the father is his own, Peleus, whom Priam has just named. ὑφ’ … ὦρσε is ὑπό with the aorist of ὄρνυμι ‘rouse’, the preposition parted from its verb (tmesis); ἵμερον is ‘longing’, with the genitive γόοιο ‘for lament’, that is, a longing to weep. The line is shared with the Odyssey. The same ἵμερος is what leaves him at 514.

sentences.t: ἁψάμενος δ’ ἄρα χειρὸς ἀπώσατο ἦκα γέροντα.
sentences.tr: hapsamenos d’ ara cheiros apōsato ēka geronta.
sentences.l: And taking hold, then, of the hand, he pushed away gently the old man.
sentences.i: Taking the old man by the hand, he gently pushed him away.
sentences.n: ἁψάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἅπτω, ‘having taken hold of’, with the genitive χειρός ‘by the hand’ (the part taken hold of). The Greek does not say whose hand, but the old man is the one raised by the hand at 515. ἀπώσατο is the aorist middle of ἀπωθέω ‘push away’, and ἦκα ‘gently, softly’ qualifies it: he puts Priam off, but kindly. ἄρα (ἄρ’) is the particle ‘then’; γέροντα is the accusative of γέρων ‘old man’.

sentences.t:
τὼ δὲ μνησαμένω ὃ μὲν Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο
κλαῖ’ ἁδινὰ προπάροιθε ποδῶν Ἀχιλῆος ἐλυσθείς,
αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεὺς κλαῖεν ἑὸν πατέρ’, ἄλλοτε δ’ αὖτε
Πάτροκλον·
sentences.tr:
tō de mnēsamenō ho men Hektoros androphonoio
klai’ hadina proparoithe podōn Achilēos elystheis,
autar Achilleus klaien heon pater’, allote d’ aute
Patroklon·
sentences.l:
And the two, having remembered, the one of Hector, man-slaying,
wept heavily, before the feet of Achilles huddled,
but Achilles wept for his own father, and at another time again
Patroclus;
sentences.i: Both were remembering: Priam wept heavily for man-slaying Hector, huddled at the feet of Achilles, while Achilles wept for his own father, and then again for Patroclus;
sentences.n: τὼ … μνησαμένω is dual, ‘the two of them, remembering’; ὃ μέν ‘the one’ is Priam, set against αὐτὰρ Ἀχιλλεύς ‘but Achilles’. Ἕκτορος ἀνδροφόνοιο is ‘man-slaying Hector’ (ἀνήρ + the root of φόνος), the stock epithet, in the genitive after μνησαμένω and as the thing wept for. κλαῖ’ is κλαῖε, the imperfect of κλαίω ‘weep’ with the augment dropped, and κλαῖεν is the same verb; ἁδινά is the adverb ‘heavily’ (literally ‘thickly’). ἐλυσθείς, the aorist passive participle of εἰλύω ‘roll up, curl up’, shows Priam huddled at Achilles’ feet. ἑόν is the possessive ‘his own’. Πάτροκλον is the second object of κλαῖεν, understood from the line before; the unit ends mid-line 512 at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: τῶν δὲ στοναχὴ κατὰ δώματ’ ὀρώρει.
sentences.tr: tōn de stonachē kata dōmat’ orōrei.
sentences.l: and of the two the groaning through the halls had arisen.
sentences.i: and their groaning had arisen through the house.
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 512, after the ano teleia. τῶν δέ ‘and of them’ is the two men, and goes with στοναχή ‘groaning’; κατὰ δώματ’ is ‘through the house’ (the plural δώματα for one dwelling, as often). ὀρώρει is the pluperfect of ὄρνυμι ‘had arisen’, the intransitive partner of the transitive aorist ὦρσε at 507.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥα γόοιο τετάρπετο δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς,
καί οἱ ἀπὸ πραπίδων ἦλθ’ ἵμερος ἠδ’ ἀπὸ γυίων,
sentences.tr:
autar epei rha gooio tetarpeto dios Achilleus,
kai hoi apo prapidōn ēlth’ himeros ēd’ apo guiōn,
sentences.l:
But when then of lament had taken his fill heavenly Achilles,
and from his midriff went the longing and from his limbs,
sentences.i: But when heavenly Achilles had taken his fill of lament, and the longing had gone from his heart and from his limbs,
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥα is ‘but when, then’, the particle ῥα (ἄρα) marking the natural next step. τετάρπετο is the reduplicated aorist middle of τέρπω, ‘had his fill of’, with the genitive γόοιο ‘lament’; δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘heavenly Achilles’, the stock epithet. The main verb ἦλθ’ ‘went’ has ἵμερος ‘longing’ as its subject, the same longing as at 507, now leaving him: the lament has run its course. οἱ ‘for him’ is a dative of the person affected; πραπίδων ‘midriff’ is the seat of feeling, and γυίων ‘limbs’ is the epic genitive of γυῖον; ἠδ’ is ‘and’. The sentence goes on to 515.

sentences.t:
αὐτίκ’ ἀπὸ θρόνου ὦρτο, γέροντα δὲ χειρὸς ἀνίστη
οἰκτίρων πολιόν τε κάρη πολιόν τε γένειον,
καί μιν φωνήσας ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.tr:
autik’ apo thronou ōrto, geronta de cheiros anistē
oiktirōn polion te karē polion te geneion,
kai min phōnēsas epea pteroenta prosēuda·
sentences.l:
at once from his chair he sprang up, and the old man by the hand he raised,
pitying his grey head and his grey beard,
and, lifting his voice, to him winged words he spoke:
sentences.i: At once he sprang up from his chair and raised the old man by the hand, pitying his grey head and his grey beard, and lifting his voice he spoke winged words to him:
sentences.n: ὦρτο is the aorist middle of ὄρνυμι, intransitive here, ‘sprang up’ (the verb of 507 and 512). ἀνίστη is the imperfect of the transitive ἀνίστημι, ‘was raising’; γέροντα … χειρός is ‘the old man by the hand’. οἰκτίρων ‘pitying’ takes two accusatives, with τε … τε ‘both … and’ and πολιόν ‘grey’ said twice in the Greek: ‘his grey head and his grey beard’ (γένειον is the chin, and the beard on it). μιν ‘him’ is Priam; this line of speech-introduction also stands at 1.201, where it is said to a goddess, hence ‘to her’ there and ‘to him’ here.

sentences.t: ἆ δείλ’, ἦ δὴ πολλὰ κάκ’ ἄνσχεο σὸν κατὰ θυμόν.
sentences.tr: a deil’, ē dē polla kak’ anscheo son kata thymon.
sentences.l: “Oh, miserable one, truly indeed many evils you held out in your heart.
sentences.i: “Oh, miserable man, you have indeed borne many evils in your heart.
sentences.n: Achilles’ speech begins. ἆ δείλ’ is a cry of address, ‘oh, miserable one’: δείλ’ is the elided vocative of δειλός, here ‘miserable, pitiable’, not ‘cowardly’. ἦ δή is ‘truly indeed’. κάκ’ is κακά ‘evils’, the object of ἄνσχεο, the second person singular aorist middle of ἀνέχομαι ‘hold out, bear’ (the same spelling is the imperative at 549). σὸν κατὰ θυμόν ‘in your heart’, with κατά ‘in, throughout’.

sentences.l:
How did you bring yourself to the ships of the Achaeans to come, alone,
into the eyes of a man who many, and good,
sons of yours I despoiled?
sentences.i: How did you bring yourself to come alone to the ships of the Achaeans, before the eyes of a man who killed and stripped so many of your good sons?
sentences.n: πῶς ἔτλης with an infinitive is ‘how did you bring yourself to …’: τλάω is ‘endure, bring oneself to’; ἐλθέμεν is the epic infinitive of ἔρχομαι, and οἶος ‘alone’ agrees with the subject. ἀνδρὸς ἐς ὀφθαλμούς is ‘into the eyes of a man’; the man is Achilles himself, and the relative clause slips into the first person, ὅς … ἐξενάριξα ‘who … I killed and stripped of their armour’ (aorist of ἐξεναρίζω), which the English cannot show. πολέας and υἱέας are the epic accusative plurals of πολύς and υἱός; τοι is σοι, ‘your’. The ‘;’ is the Greek question mark; the unit ends mid-line 521.

sentences.t: σιδήρειόν νύ τοι ἦτορ.
sentences.tr: sidēreion ny toi ētor.
sentences.l: Iron, then, is your heart.
sentences.i: Your heart is iron.
sentences.n: This sentence begins mid-line 521, after the question mark. σιδήρειον ‘of iron’ is the predicate and ἦτορ ‘heart’ the subject; νύ is ‘then, indeed’ and τοι is σοι ‘your’. A heart that can face the killer of its sons is of iron: pity and reproach together.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ κατ’ ἄρ’ ἕζευ ἐπὶ θρόνου, ἄλγεα δ’ ἔμπης
ἐν θυμῷ κατακεῖσθαι ἐάσομεν ἀχνύμενοί περ·
sentences.tr:
all’ age dē kat’ ar’ hezeu epi thronou, algea d’ empēs
en thymōi katakeisthai easomen achnymenoi per·
sentences.l:
But come now, sit down then upon the chair, and pains all the same
in the heart to lie we will allow, grieving though we are;
sentences.i: But come now, sit down on the chair; all the same we will let our pains lie in our hearts, grieving though we are;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is ‘but come now’. ἕζευ is the imperative of ἕζομαι ‘sit’, with κατά (κατ’ … ἕζευ) ‘sit down’; θρόνου ‘chair’ is the seat Priam is asked to take. ἔμπης ‘all the same’ goes with ἐάσομεν ‘we will let’, either the future or the epic short-vowel subjunctive ‘let us let’; the sense, a joint resolve, is the same. κατακεῖσθαι is the infinitive of κάτακειμαι ‘lie’, with ἄλγεα ‘pains’ as its subject and ἐν θυμῷ ‘in the heart’. ἀχνύμενοί περ is ‘grieving though we are’, nominative plural.

sentences.t: οὐ γάρ τις πρῆξις πέλεται κρυεροῖο γόοιο·
sentences.tr: ou gar tis prēxis peletai kryeroio gooio·
sentences.l: for no accomplishment comes from chilling lament;
sentences.i: for nothing is accomplished by chilling lament;
sentences.n: γάρ ‘for’ gives the reason. πρῆξις (from πράσσω) is ‘a doing, an achieving’, so ‘no accomplishment’, and πέλεται is ‘comes to be, is’. The genitive κρυεροῖο γόοιο ‘chilling lament’ names what it does not come from; κρυερός ‘chilling’ is from κρύος ‘frost’, and the phrase is a set one for a lament that freezes the mourner.

sentences.t:
ὡς γὰρ ἐπεκλώσαντο θεοὶ δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι
ζώειν ἀχνυμένοις·
sentences.tr:
hōs gar epeklōsanto theoi deiloisi brotoisi
zōein achnymenois·
sentences.l:
for so the gods spun for miserable mortals
to live grieving;
sentences.i: for so the gods have spun it for miserable mortals: to live in grief;
sentences.n: ὡς ‘so, thus’ looks forward to the infinitive ζώειν: so the gods have spun it, that they live grieving. ἐπεκλώσαντο is the aorist middle of ἐπικλώθω ‘spin to’, the thread of each life spun by the gods. δειλοῖσι βροτοῖσι is ‘miserable mortals’ (the epic dative plural; δειλός as at 518, not ‘cowardly’). ζώειν is the epic infinitive of ζώω ‘live’ (Attic ζῆν), and ἀχνυμένοις ‘grieving’ agrees with βροτοῖσι. The unit ends mid-line 526 at the ano teleia.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ δέ τ’ ἀκηδέες εἰσί.
sentences.tr: autoi de t’ akēdees eisi.
sentences.l: but themselves they are uncaring.
sentences.i: while they themselves are uncaring.
sentences.n: This sentence begins mid-line 526, after the ano teleia. αὐτοί ‘they themselves’ are the gods; δέ τ’ sets them against the mortals, and τε gives the statement the sound of a general truth. ἀκηδέες is the uncontracted nominative plural of ἀκηδής, ‘without κῆδος’, uncaring; it is active here, as of the gods who feel no grief, where at 554 it is passive, ‘uncared for’.

sentences.t:
δοιοὶ γάρ τε πίθοι κατακείαται ἐν Διὸς οὔδει
δώρων οἷα δίδωσι κακῶν, ἕτερος δὲ ἑάων·
sentences.tr:
doioi gar te pithoi katakeiatai en Dios oudei
dōrōn hoia didōsi kakōn, heteros de heaōn·
sentences.l:
For two jars lie on the floor of Zeus,
of gifts, such as he gives, of evil ones, and the other of good ones;
sentences.i: For two jars lie on the floor of Zeus, holding the gifts that he gives: the one of evils, the other of good things;
sentences.n: The fable of the two jars. δοιοί is ‘two’ and πίθοι are large storage jars; κατακείαται is the Ionic third plural (-αται for -νται) of κάτακειμαι ‘lie’. ἐν Διὸς οὔδει is ‘on the floor of Zeus’ (οὖδας ‘ground, floor’). The τε in δοιοί γάρ τε gives a general truth, and οἷα δίδωσι is ‘such as he gives’. δώρων … κακῶν ‘of gifts, of evil ones’ is said of the first jar, ἕτερος δὲ ἑάων ‘and the other of good ones’ of the second; ἑάων is the epic genitive plural of ἐΰς ‘good’.

sentences.t:
ᾧ μέν κ’ ἀμμίξας δώῃ Ζεὺς τερπικέραυνος,
ἄλλοτε μέν τε κακῷ ὅ γε κύρεται, ἄλλοτε δ’ ἐσθλῷ·
sentences.tr:
hōi men k’ ammixas dōēi Zeus terpikeraunos,
allote men te kakōi ho ge kyretai, allote d’ esthlōi·
sentences.l:
To whom, having mixed them, may give Zeus, delighting-in-the-thunderbolt,
at one time with evil that man meets, at another with good;
sentences.i: The man to whom Zeus, who delights in the thunderbolt, gives a mixture meets with evil at one time and with good at another;
sentences.n: ᾧ μέν ‘to whom, on the one hand’ is answered by ᾧ δέ at 531. ἀμμίξας is the aorist participle of ἀναμίγνυμι ‘mix up’ (ἀν- assimilated before μ), and δώῃ is the aorist subjunctive of a general relative clause, ‘to whomever he gives’. Ζεὺς τερπικέραυνος is ‘Zeus who delights in the thunderbolt’ (τέρπω ‘delight’ + κεραυνός ‘thunderbolt’), his stock epithet. κύρεται (κυρέω ‘meet, light upon’) takes the dative κακῷ … ἐσθλῷ; ἄλλοτε μέν … ἄλλοτε δ’ is ‘at one time … at another’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ᾧ δέ κε τῶν λυγρῶν δώῃ, λωβητὸν ἔθηκε,
καί ἑ κακὴ βούβρωστις ἐπὶ χθόνα δῖαν ἐλαύνει,
φοιτᾷ δ’ οὔτε θεοῖσι τετιμένος οὔτε βροτοῖσιν.
sentences.tr:
hōi de ke tōn lygrōn dōēi, lōbēton ethēke,
kai he kakē boubrōstis epi chthona dian elaunei,
phoitāi d’ oute theoisi tetimenos oute brotoisin.
sentences.l:
but to whom he gives of the grievous ones, an object of outrage he makes him,
and evil ox-hunger over the heavenly earth drives him,
and he goes to and fro, honoured neither by gods nor by mortals.
sentences.i: But the man to whom he gives of the grievous gifts he makes an object of insult; evil, ravenous hunger drives him over the heavenly earth, and he goes to and fro, honoured neither by gods nor by mortals.
sentences.n: The other half of the contrast: τῶν λυγρῶν ‘of the grievous ones’ is a partitive genitive after δώῃ, the gifts of the jar of evils. λωβητόν is ‘an object of outrage’ (λώβη ‘insult’), with ἔθηκε, an aorist of what always happens, put in the present. βούβρωστις is a rare compound, ‘ox-hunger’ (βοῦς + the root of βιβρώσκω ‘eat’); the ancient explanation is ‘ravenous hunger’, but its exact sense is not known. ἐπὶ χθόνα δῖαν is ‘over the heavenly earth’ (δῖος ‘heavenly’), and ἑ ‘him’ is the object of ἐλαύνει; ἔθηκε has no pronoun of its own, and ‘makes him’ is understood from it. φοιτᾷ is ‘goes to and fro’; τετιμένος is the perfect passive participle of τιμάω ‘honour’, and οὔτε … οὔτε ‘neither … nor’.

sentences.t:
ὣς μὲν καὶ Πηλῆϊ θεοὶ δόσαν ἀγλαὰ δῶρα
ἐκ γενετῆς·
sentences.tr:
hōs men kai Pēlēï theoi dosan aglaa dōra
ek genetēs·
sentences.l:
So indeed to Peleus also the gods gave splendid gifts
from birth;
sentences.i: So it was with Peleus too: the gods gave him splendid gifts from his birth;
sentences.n: Achilles applies the fable to his own father. ὣς μὲν καί is ‘so indeed also’; Πηλῆϊ is the epic dative of Πηλεύς ‘Peleus’, and δόσαν is ἔδοσαν, the aorist of δίδωσι with the augment dropped. ἀγλαὰ δῶρα is ‘splendid gifts’, and ἐκ γενετῆς ‘from birth’ (γενετή). The gifts are those of the good jar, listed in the next lines; the unit ends mid-line 535 at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
πάντας γὰρ ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους ἐκέκαστο
ὄλβῳ τε πλούτῳ τε, ἄνασσε δὲ Μυρμιδόνεσσι,
καί οἱ θνητῷ ἐόντι θεὰν ποίησαν ἄκοιτιν.
sentences.tr:
pantas gar ep’ anthrōpous ekekasto
olbōi te ploutōi te, anasse de Myrmidonessi,
kai hoi thnētōi eonti thean poiēsan akoitin.
sentences.l:
for above all men he excelled
in prosperity and wealth, and was lord over the Myrmidons,
and to him, a mortal being, a goddess they made a wife.
sentences.i: for he excelled all men in prosperity and wealth, and was lord over the Myrmidons, and they made a goddess his wife, mortal though he was.
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 535, after the ano teleia. ἐκέκαστο is the pluperfect of καίνυμαι ‘excel’, with ἐπί and the accusative, ‘above all men’. ὄλβῳ τε πλούτῳ τε is ‘in prosperity and in wealth’ (datives of respect); ἄνασσε is the imperfect of ἀνάσσω ‘be lord’, with the dative Μυρμιδόνεσσι (epic -εσσι) ‘over the Myrmidons’. θεάν is ‘goddess’, the sea-goddess who is Achilles’ mother, described at 562; ἐόντι is the epic form of ὄντι. οἱ … ποίησαν ‘they made for him’ has the gods of 534 as its subject, and ἄκοιτις is ‘wife’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἐπὶ καὶ τῷ θῆκε θεὸς κακόν, ὅττί οἱ οὔ τι
παίδων ἐν μεγάροισι γονὴ γένετο κρειόντων,
ἀλλ’ ἕνα παῖδα τέκεν παναώριον·
sentences.tr:
all’ epi kai tōi thēke theos kakon, hotti hoi ou ti
paidōn en megaroisi gonē geneto kreiontōn,
all’ hena paida teken panaōrion·
sentences.i: But a god laid an evil on him too: that in his halls no offspring of ruling children came to be for him, but she bore one child only, wholly untimely;
sentences.n: ἐπὶ … θῆκε is ‘laid upon’ (tmesis) and καὶ τῷ is ‘on him too’ (τῷ, Peleus). ὅττι is ὅτι ‘that’, naming the evil: οὔ τι γονὴ γένετο ‘no offspring came to be’, παίδων … κρειόντων ‘of ruling children’ (the participle of κρείω, the verb behind κρείων ‘lord’), so a line of princes to follow him. μεγάροισι is the epic dative plural of μέγαρον ‘hall’. τέκεν is ‘she bore’; the subject, Thetis, is left unnamed. παναώριον is πάν ‘wholly’ + ἀώριος ‘out of season, untimely’: a son whose time is cut short, Achilles speaking of himself. The unit ends mid-line 540 at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ νυ τόν γε
γηράσκοντα κομίζω, ἐπεὶ μάλα τηλόθι πάτρης
ἧμαι ἐνὶ Τροίῃ, σέ τε κήδων ἠδὲ σὰ τέκνα.
sentences.tr:
oude ny ton ge
gēraskonta komizō, epei mala tēlothi patrēs
hēmai eni Troiēi, se te kēdōn ēde sa tekna.
sentences.l:
and not indeed him at least
growing old do I tend, since very far from my fatherland
I sit in Troy, distressing you and your children.
sentences.i: and I do not tend him as he grows old, since I sit in Troy very far from my fatherland, distressing you and your children.
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 540. οὐδέ νυ τόν γε is ‘and not him, at least’, the son, Achilles himself. γηράσκοντα is the participle of γηράσκω ‘grow old’, and κομίζω is ‘I look after, tend’. ἐπεί ‘since’ gives the reason; τηλόθι πάτρης is ‘far from the fatherland’ and ἧμαι ‘I sit’ (a present, with a middle ending); Τροίῃ is the epic dative of Τροία. κήδων is the participle of κήδω ‘distress’ with two objects, σέ and σὰ τέκνα ‘you and your children’: Achilles’ presence at Troy is what troubles Priam’s house.

sentences.t: καὶ σὲ γέρον τὸ πρὶν μὲν ἀκούομεν ὄλβιον εἶναι·
sentences.tr: kai se geron to prin men akouomen olbion einai·
sentences.l: And you also, old man, formerly we hear to have been prosperous;
sentences.i: You too, old man, we hear were prosperous once;
sentences.n: Achilles turns from Peleus to Priam. καὶ σέ ‘you too’; τὸ πρίν is ‘before, formerly’, and μέν is answered by αὐτάρ at 547. ἀκούομεν ‘we hear’ is a plural whose ‘we’ the Greek does not define, and the infinitive εἶναι is tenseless in the Greek, so ‘were’ is the sense that τὸ πρίν requires. ὄλβιον ‘prosperous’ is the accusative agreeing with σέ.

sentences.t:
ὅσσον Λέσβος ἄνω Μάκαρος ἕδος ἐντὸς ἐέργει
καὶ Φρυγίη καθύπερθε καὶ Ἑλλήσποντος ἀπείρων,
τῶν σε γέρον πλούτῳ τε καὶ υἱάσι φασὶ κεκάσθαι.
sentences.tr:
hosson Lesbos anō Makaros hedos entos eergei
kai Phrygiē kathyperthe kai Hellēspontos apeirōn,
tōn se geron ploutōi te kai huiasi phasi kekasthai.
sentences.l:
As much as Lesbos, seat of Makar, above shuts in within,
and Phrygia beyond, and the boundless Hellespont,
of these, old man, in wealth and in sons they say you excelled.
sentences.i: Of all that Lesbos, seat of Makar, shuts in from above, and Phrygia beyond it, and the boundless Hellespont: of all these, old man, they say you excelled in wealth and in sons.
sentences.n: Priam’s old realm is drawn by its limits. ὅσσον ‘as much as’ begins the measure; Λέσβος … Μάκαρος ἕδος is ‘Lesbos, the seat of Makar’, Makar is named without explanation (tradition makes him an early ruler of the island); ἄνω ‘above’ and ἐντός ‘within’ are directions the poet does not make plain, and ἐέργει is ‘shuts in, bounds’. καθύπερθε ‘above, further up’ goes with Φρυγίη; Ἑλλήσποντος ἀπείρων is ‘the boundless Hellespont’ (ἄπειρος ‘without limit’). τῶν σε … κεκάσθαι: κεκάσθαι is the perfect infinitive of καίνυμαι ‘excel’ (compare ἐκέκαστο at 535), with the genitive τῶν ‘of these’, whether lands or peoples the Greek does not decide; φασί ‘they say’ governs it, and υἱάσι is the epic dative plural of υἱός.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί τοι πῆμα τόδ’ ἤγαγον Οὐρανίωνες
αἰεί τοι περὶ ἄστυ μάχαι τ’ ἀνδροκτασίαι τε.
sentences.tr:
autar epei toi pēma tod’ ēgagon Ouraniōnes
aiei toi peri asty machai t’ androktasiai te.
sentences.l:
But since upon you this woe brought the Uranians,
always around your city are battles and man-slayings.
sentences.i: But since the gods of heaven brought this woe on you, there are always battles and man-slayings around your city.
sentences.n: αὐτάρ answers the μέν of 543: ‘you were prosperous once, but since …’. τοι is σοι ‘on you’; πῆμα is ‘woe’, and ἤγαγον ‘brought’ is the aorist of ἄγω. Οὐρανίωνες is ‘the Uranians’, the descendants of Οὐρανός ‘Heaven’, that is, the gods of heaven. The second line has no verb, which is supplied: ‘there are always battles …’; μάχαι ‘battles’ and ἀνδροκτασίαι ‘man-slayings’ (ἀνήρ + the root of κτείνω ‘kill’) are paired with τε … τε ‘both … and’.

sentences.t: ἄνσχεο, μὴ δ’ ἀλίαστον ὀδύρεο σὸν κατὰ θυμόν·
sentences.tr: anscheo, mē d’ aliaston odyreo son kata thymon·
sentences.l: Hold out, and not relentlessly lament in your heart;
sentences.i: Bear up, and do not lament relentlessly in your heart;
sentences.n: ἄνσχεο is here the aorist imperative of ἀνέχομαι ‘hold out, bear up’, where at 518 the same spelling was the indicative. μὴ δ’ is the edition’s spelling of μηδέ ‘and not’, with ὀδύρεο, the imperative of ὀδύρομαι ‘lament’ (-εο for -ου). ἀλίαστον is the adverbial accusative of ἀλίαστος ‘relentless’, a rare word whose sense is traditional rather than certain. σὸν κατὰ θυμόν ‘in your heart’ as at 518.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ τι πρήξεις ἀκαχήμενος υἷος ἑῆος,
οὐδέ μιν ἀνστήσεις, πρὶν καὶ κακὸν ἄλλο πάθῃσθα.
sentences.tr:
ou gar ti prēxeis akachēmenos huios heēos,
oude min anstēseis, prin kai kakon allo pathēistha.
sentences.l:
for you will accomplish nothing grieved for your own son,
nor will you raise him up, before also some other evil you suffer.”
sentences.i: for you will achieve nothing by grieving for your own son, and you will not raise him up before you suffer some other evil as well.”
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ τι πρήξεις is ‘for you will accomplish nothing’ (future of πράσσω, answering πρῆξις at 524). ἀκαχήμενος is a perfect middle participle, ‘grieved’, with the genitive υἷος ἑῆος ‘for your son’; ἑῆος is the epic genitive of the possessive ἑός ‘one’s own’, though some take it as a genitive of ἐΰς ‘good’, so the sense may be ‘your good son’. μιν ‘him’; ἀνστήσεις is the future of ἀνίστημι ‘make stand up’, here from the dead. πρὶν καὶ … πάθῃσθα is πρίν with the subjunctive (no ἄν after a negative main clause), ‘before you suffer’, the second person ending -σθα being epic. The closing mark ends Achilles’ speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἠμείβετ’ ἔπειτα γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ēmeibet’ epeita gerōn Priamos theoeidēs·
sentences.l: Him then answered the old man Priam, godlike in form:
sentences.i: Then Priam, the old man, godlike in form, answered him:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction: τὸν ‘him’ is Achilles, and ἠμείβετο is the imperfect of ἀμείβομαι ‘answer’. γέρων Πρίαμος θεοειδής is ‘the old man Priam, godlike in form’ (θεός + εἶδος ‘form’), the epithet kept every time.

sentences.t:
μή πω μ’ ἐς θρόνον ἵζε διοτρεφὲς ὄφρά κεν Ἕκτωρ
κεῖται ἐνὶ κλισίῃσιν ἀκηδής, ἀλλὰ τάχιστα
λῦσον ἵν’ ὀφθαλμοῖσιν ἴδω·
sentences.tr:
mē pō m’ es thronon hize diotrephes ophra ken Hektōr
keitai eni klisiēisin akēdēs, alla tachista
lyson hin’ ophthalmoisin idō·
sentences.i: “Do not yet make me sit on a chair, Zeus-nurtured one, while Hector lies uncared for in the huts, but release him as quickly as possible, so that I may see him with my eyes;
sentences.n: Priam’s refusal to sit. μή … ἵζε is a prohibition in the present imperative, ‘do not (go on to) seat me’, with ἵζω used transitively, and μή πω is ‘not yet’; ἐς θρόνον ‘onto a chair’. διοτρεφές is the vocative of διοτρεφής ‘Zeus-nurtured’, an honorific. ὄφρα κεν … κεῖται is ‘so long as … lies’, and ἐνὶ κλισίῃσιν ‘in the huts’ (κλισίη ‘hut’). ἀκηδής ‘uncared for’ means untended, unburied (compare ἀκηδέες at 526). λῦσον, the aorist imperative of λύω, is ‘release’, the word for giving up a body for ransom; ἵν’ … ἴδω is a purpose clause with the aorist subjunctive, and ὀφθαλμοῖσιν is ‘with the eyes’. The unit ends mid-line 555 at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ δέξαι ἄποινα
πολλά, τά τοι φέρομεν·
sentences.tr:
sy de dexai apoina
polla, ta toi pheromen·
sentences.l:
and you, accept the ransom,
much, which to you we bring;
sentences.i: and you, accept the ransom, a great deal of it, that we bring you;
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 555 and ends mid-line 556. δέξαι is the aorist imperative of δέχομαι ‘accept’; ἄποινα πολλά is ‘much ransom’; τά is the relative ‘which’, τοι is σοι ‘to you’, and φέρομεν ‘we bring’ is plural, Priam speaking for his party.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ τῶνδ’ ἀπόναιο, καὶ ἔλθοις
σὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν, ἐπεί με πρῶτον ἔασας
αὐτόν τε ζώειν καὶ ὁρᾶν φάος ἠελίοιο.
sentences.tr:
sy de tōnd’ aponaio, kai elthois
sēn es patrida gaian, epei me prōton easas
auton te zōein kai horan phaos ēelioio.
sentences.l:
and you, may you have enjoyment of these, and may you come
to your fatherland, since me first you allowed
myself both to live and to see the light of the sun.”
sentences.i: and may you enjoy these things, and come to your fatherland, since you first allowed me myself to live and to see the light of the sun.”
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 556. ἀπόναιο is the aorist optative middle of ἀπονίνημι ‘have the good of’, with the genitive τῶνδ’ ‘of these’, the ransom; ἔλθοις is the aorist optative ‘may you come’, both wishes. σὴν ἐς πατρίδα γαῖαν is ‘to your fatherland’. ἐπεί με πρῶτον ἔασας is ‘since you first let me’, ἔασας being the aorist of ἐάω ‘allow’, with the infinitives ζώειν ‘to live’ and ὁρᾶν ‘to see’ and με … αὐτόν ‘me myself’ as their subject. φάος ἠελίοιο is ‘the light of the sun’ (ἠελίοιο, epic genitive of ἥλιος). The closing mark ends Priam’s speech.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπόδρα ἰδὼν προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ ar’ hypodra idōn prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him then with a scowl looking addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: Then Achilles, swift of foot, looking at him with a scowl, spoke to him:
sentences.n: A speech-introduction. ὑπόδρα ἰδών is ‘looking from under (the brows)’, a scowl; the exact derivation of ὑπόδρα is not certain. προσέφη is ‘addressed’, and πόδας ὠκύς ‘swift in the feet’ (an accusative of respect) is Achilles’ stock epithet.

sentences.t: μηκέτι νῦν μ’ ἐρέθιζε γέρον·
sentences.tr: mēketi nyn m’ erethize geron·
sentences.l: “No longer now provoke me, old man;
sentences.i: “Do not provoke me any more now, old man;
sentences.n: μηκέτι ‘no longer’ with the present imperative ἐρέθιζε (ἐρεθίζω ‘provoke’) is ‘stop provoking me’. Agamemnon’s words to Chryses at 1.32, μή μ’ ἐρέθιζε, are close to these. γέρον is the vocative of γέρων. The unit ends mid-line 560 at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
νοέω δὲ καὶ αὐτὸς
Ἕκτορά τοι λῦσαι, Διόθεν δέ μοι ἄγγελος ἦλθε
μήτηρ, ἥ μ’ ἔτεκεν, θυγάτηρ ἁλίοιο γέροντος.
sentences.tr:
noeō de kai autos
Hektora toi lysai, Diothen de moi angelos ēlthe
mētēr, hē m’ eteken, thygatēr halioio gerontos.
sentences.l:
and I have in mind, myself also,
to release Hector to you, and from Zeus to me a messenger came,
my mother, who bore me, the daughter of the old man of the sea.
sentences.i: and I myself have it in mind to release Hector to you; a messenger came to me from Zeus, my mother, who bore me, the daughter of the old man of the sea.
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 560. νοέω with an infinitive is ‘I have in mind to’ (νοέω ‘perceive, think’); καὶ αὐτός is ‘I too, of myself’. Ἕκτορά τοι λῦσαι is ‘to release Hector for you’ (τοι = σοι). Διόθεν is ‘from Zeus’ (the ending -θεν marks the source), and μήτηρ is in apposition to ἄγγελος ‘messenger’. ἥ μ’ ἔτεκεν is ‘who bore me’; θυγάτηρ ἁλίοιο γέροντος is ‘daughter of the old man of the sea’, Thetis’ stock description, with her father not named.

sentences.t:
καὶ δέ σε γιγνώσκω Πρίαμε φρεσίν, οὐδέ με λήθεις,
ὅττι θεῶν τίς σ’ ἦγε θοὰς ἐπὶ νῆας Ἀχαιῶν.
sentences.tr:
kai de se gignōskō Priame phresin, oude me lētheis,
hotti theōn tis s’ ēge thoas epi nēas Achaiōn.
sentences.l:
And you also I recognise, Priam, in my wits, and you do not escape me,
that some one of the gods led you to the swift ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.i: And I recognise you too, Priam, in my mind, and it does not escape me that one of the gods led you to the swift ships of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: καὶ δέ is ‘and moreover’; γιγνώσκω is ‘I recognise’, with φρεσίν ‘in my wits, in my mind’ (epic dative plural of φρήν). οὐδέ με λήθεις is ‘and you do not escape my notice’ (λανθάνω with the accusative of the person); ὅττι is ὅτι ‘that’, opening what he has seen through: θεῶν τίς ‘some one of the gods’. ἦγε is the imperfect of ἄγω ‘led’, and θοάς ‘swift’ is the stock epithet of ships.

sentences.t:
οὐ γάρ κε τλαίη βροτὸς ἐλθέμεν, οὐδὲ μάλ’ ἡβῶν,
ἐς στρατόν·
sentences.tr:
ou gar ke tlaiē brotos elthemen, oude mal’ hēbōn,
es straton·
sentences.l:
For no mortal would bring himself to come, nor quite in youthful prime,
into the army;
sentences.i: for no mortal, not even one fully in youthful prime, would bring himself to come into the army;
sentences.n: οὐ γάρ κε τλαίη is a potential optative with κε, ‘no one would bring himself’ (τλάω as at 519), with βροτός ‘mortal’ as subject and ἐλθέμεν ‘to come’. οὐδὲ μάλ’ ἡβῶν is ‘not even one fully in youthful prime’ (ἡβάω ‘be in youthful prime’); even a man in full youth could not do it. ἐς στρατόν is ‘into the army’, the camp. The unit ends mid-line 566 at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν φυλάκους λάθοι, οὐδέ κ’ ὀχῆα
ῥεῖα μετοχλίσσειε θυράων ἡμετεράων.
sentences.tr:
oude gar an phylakous lathoi, oude k’ ochēa
rheia metochlisseie thyraōn hēmeteraōn.
sentences.l:
for neither could he escape the notice of the guards, nor the bar
easily would he lever back of our doors.
sentences.i: for he would not escape the notice of the guards, nor could he easily force back the bar of our doors.
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 566. οὐδὲ γὰρ ἂν … λάθοι is ‘for neither would he escape the notice of’, an optative with ἄν, with φυλάκους, the accusative plural of φύλαξ ‘guard’ in the form the edition prints. οὐδέ κ’ … μετοχλίσσειε is another potential optative, ‘nor could he … lever back’, from μετά + ὀχλίζω ‘move with a lever’ (compare μοχλός ‘bar, lever’); ὀχῆα is ‘the bar’. ῥεῖα ‘easily’; θυράων ἡμετεράων is ‘of our doors’, the epic genitive plural of θύρα and ἡμέτερος.

sentences.t:
τὼ νῦν μή μοι μᾶλλον ἐν ἄλγεσι θυμὸν ὀρίνῃς,
μή σε γέρον οὐδ’ αὐτὸν ἐνὶ κλισίῃσιν ἐάσω
καὶ ἱκέτην περ ἐόντα, Διὸς δ’ ἀλίτωμαι ἐφετμάς.
sentences.tr:
tō nyn mē moi mallon en algesi thymon orinēis,
mē se geron oud’ auton eni klisiēisin easō
kai hiketēn per eonta, Dios d’ alitōmai ephetmas.
sentences.l:
So now do not for me further among my pains stir my heart,
lest I leave you not, old man, even yourself, in the huts,
suppliant though you are, and I offend against the commands of Zeus.”
sentences.i: So now do not stir my heart any further among my pains, or I may fail to leave you in peace, old man, even you, in my huts, suppliant though you are, and may offend against the commands of Zeus.”
sentences.n: τώ ‘therefore’; μή μοι … ὀρίνῃς is a prohibition with the aorist subjunctive, ‘do not stir my heart’ (ὀρίνω ‘stir’), μοι being ‘for me’ and ἐν ἄλγεσι ‘among pains’. Then μή … ἐάσω … ἀλίτωμαι is a fear clause: ἐάσω is from ἐάω ‘let be, leave alone’, and the Greek says only that he might not ‘let you be’, what he would do being left to be understood. οὐδ’ αὐτόν is ‘not even you yourself’, ἱκέτην περ ἐόντα is ‘though you are a suppliant’ (περ concessive, ἐόντα = ὄντα), and ἀλίτωμαι is the aorist subjunctive of ἀλιτραίνω ‘offend against, sin against’, with Διὸς … ἐφετμάς ‘the commands of Zeus’. The closing mark ends Achilles’ speech.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, ἔδεισεν δ’ ὃ γέρων καὶ ἐπείθετο μύθῳ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, edeisen d’ ho gerōn kai epeitheto mythōi.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and the old man was afraid and obeyed the word;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the old man was afraid and did as he was told.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ closes the speech. ὁ γέρων is ‘the old man’, the article used as a demonstrative, and ἔδεισεν is the aorist of δείδω ‘fear’. ἐπείθετο is the imperfect of πείθομαι ‘obey’, with the dative μύθῳ ‘the word’. The line is shared with 1.33, where Chryses is the old man.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ οἴκοιο λέων ὣς ἆλτο θύραζε
οὐκ οἶος,
sentences.tr:
Pēleïdēs d’ oikoio leōn hōs alto thyraze
ouk oios,
sentences.l:
And Peleus’-son from the house, like a lion, leapt outside,
not alone,
sentences.i: The son of Peleus sprang out of the house like a lion, and not alone,
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης is the patronymic ‘son of Peleus’, here Achilles. οἴκοιο is a genitive of separation, ‘from the house’ (epic -οιο = Attic -ου); λέων ὣς is ‘like a lion’ with the particle after its noun. ἆλτο is the aorist of ἅλλομαι ‘leap’, and θύραζε is ‘to the outside’ (-ζε is ‘to’). οὐκ οἶος ‘not alone’ leads to the two who followed, in the next unit, which begins mid-line 573.

sentences.t:
ἅμα τῷ γε δύω θεράποντες ἕποντο
ἥρως Αὐτομέδων ἠδ’ Ἄλκιμος, οὕς ῥα μάλιστα
τῖ’ Ἀχιλεὺς ἑτάρων μετὰ Πάτροκλόν γε θανόντα,
sentences.tr:
hama tōi ge dyō therapontes heponto
hērōs Automedōn ēd’ Alkimos, hous rha malista
ti’ Achileus hetarōn meta Patroklon ge thanonta,
sentences.l:
together with him two attendants followed,
the hero Automedon and Alcimus, whom then especially
Achilles honoured of his companions after Patroclus, dead,
sentences.i: two attendants followed with him, the hero Automedon and Alcimus, whom Achilles honoured most of his companions, next after Patroclus, now dead,
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 573. ἅμα τῷ γε is ‘along with him’, δύω ‘two’, θεράποντες ‘attendants’ and ἕποντο the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’; ἥρως ‘hero’ is a title, set before Αὐτομέδων. οὕς ῥα μάλιστα τῖ’ is ‘whom then most … honoured’, τῖ’ being the imperfect of τίω ‘honour’ without its augment; ἑτάρων is the genitive ‘of his companions’. μετὰ Πάτροκλον … θανόντα is ‘next after Patroclus, dead’: μετά with the accusative can mean after in rank and after in time, and both are in play. Ἀχιλεύς has the single λ.

sentences.t:
οἳ τόθ’ ὑπὸ ζυγόφιν λύον ἵππους ἡμιόνους τε,
ἐς δ’ ἄγαγον κήρυκα καλήτορα τοῖο γέροντος,
sentences.tr:
hoi toth’ hypo zygophin lyon hippous hēmionous te,
es d’ agagon kēryka kalētora toio gerontos,
sentences.l:
who then from under the yoke loosed horses and mules,
and led in the herald, the caller, of that old man,
sentences.i: who then loosed the horses and mules from under the yoke, and led in the herald, the crier of that old man,
sentences.n: οἳ τόθ’ ‘who then’ takes up the two attendants. ὑπὸ ζυγόφιν is ‘from under the yoke’, the ending -φιν marking the place from which; λύον is ‘loosed’ (imperfect, augment dropped), and ἵππους ἡμιόνους τε is ‘horses and mules’. ἐς … ἄγαγον is ‘led in’ (the preposition ἐς parted from its verb, tmesis); the herald is the one who came with Priam. καλήτορα is ‘caller’ (from καλέω ‘call’), a rare word; τοῖο is the epic genitive of the demonstrative ‘that’.

sentences.t: κὰδ δ’ ἐπὶ δίφρου εἷσαν·
sentences.tr: kad d’ epi diphrou heisan·
sentences.l: and down upon a stool they seated him;
sentences.i: and sat him down on a stool;
sentences.n: κὰδ … εἷσαν is ‘seated down’: κάδ is κατά with its last letter taken over by the δ that follows, and εἷσαν is the aorist of ἵζω, here transitive, ‘made sit’. ἐπὶ δίφρου ‘on a stool’; δίφρος is the chariot-board and also, as here, a seat. The one seated is the herald of the line before. The unit ends mid-line 578 at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
ἐϋξέστου δ’ ἀπ’ ἀπήνης
ᾕρεον Ἑκτορέης κεφαλῆς ἀπερείσι’ ἄποινα.
sentences.tr:
eÿxestou d’ ap’ apēnēs
hēireon Hektoreēs kephalēs apereisi’ apoina.
sentences.l:
and from the well-polished wagon
they took off the unstinted ransom for Hector’s head.
sentences.i: and from the well-polished wagon they took down the unstinted ransom for Hector’s head.
sentences.n: This unit begins mid-line 578. ἐϋξέστου ‘well-polished’ (the edition prints the diaeresis), ἀπήνης ‘of the wagon’; ἀπ’ … ᾕρεον is the imperfect of ἀφαιρέω ‘take off’, with the preposition parted from its verb. Ἑκτορέης κεφαλῆς is ‘for Hector’s head’, the adjective Ἑκτορέης standing for the genitive of the name, and the head for the man; ἀπερείσι’ is ἀπερείσια ‘unstinted’. The same words describe the loading of the wagon at 24.276.

sentences.t:
κὰδ δ’ ἔλιπον δύο φάρε’ ἐΰννητόν τε χιτῶνα,
ὄφρα νέκυν πυκάσας δοίη οἶκον δὲ φέρεσθαι.
sentences.tr:
kad d’ elipon dyo phare’ eÿnnēton te chitōna,
ophra nekyn pykasas doiē oikon de pheresthai.
sentences.l:
and down they left two cloaks and a well-spun tunic,
so that, having covered the corpse, he might give it to carry home.
sentences.i: and left behind two cloaks and a well-spun tunic, so that he could cover the corpse and give it to be carried home.
sentences.n: κὰδ … ἔλιπον is ‘they left behind’ (κάδ = κατά ‘down’, with the aorist of λείπω); δύο φάρε’ is ‘two cloaks’ (φάρεα elided); ἐΰννητον is ‘well-spun’ and χιτῶνα ‘tunic’. ὄφρα with the optative δοίη ‘so that he might give’ is a purpose clause, the subject being Achilles; πυκάσας is the aorist participle of πυκάζω ‘cover closely’, and νέκυν is ‘the corpse’. οἶκον δέ is ‘homewards’ and φέρεσθαι the middle infinitive ‘to carry off’; the one who carries it, Priam, is not named.

sentences.t:
δμῳὰς δ’ ἐκκαλέσας λοῦσαι κέλετ’ ἀμφί τ’ ἀλεῖψαι
νόσφιν ἀειράσας, ὡς μὴ Πρίαμος ἴδοι υἱόν,
sentences.tr:
dmōias d’ ekkalesas lousai kelet’ amphi t’ aleipsai
nosphin aeirasas, hōs mē Priamos idoi huion,
sentences.l:
and the maidservants, having called out, to wash he bade, and to anoint,
apart having lifted him, so that Priam might not see his son,
sentences.i: He called out the maids and bade them wash the body and anoint it, lifting it away to one side so that Priam might not see his son,
sentences.n: δμῳάς is the accusative plural of δμῳή ‘maidservant’; ἐκκαλέσας ‘having called out’ (of the house) is an aorist participle, and κέλετ’ is ἐκέλετο, ‘bade’, with the augment dropped (κέλομαι). λοῦσαι is the aorist infinitive of λούω ‘wash’, and ἀμφί τ’ ἀλεῖψαι is ‘and to anoint’, ἀμφί being the prefix of ἀλεῖψαι (tmesis) ‘anoint all over’. νόσφιν ‘apart’ goes with ἀειράσας, the aorist participle of ἀείρω ‘lift’; the participle is masculine, so Achilles himself lifts the body aside, the body being understood as object. ὡς μὴ … ἴδοι is a purpose clause with the optative, ‘so that he might not see’.

sentences.t:
μὴ ὃ μὲν ἀχνυμένῃ κραδίῃ χόλον οὐκ ἐρύσαιτο
παῖδα ἰδών, Ἀχιλῆϊ δ’ ὀρινθείη φίλον ἦτορ,
καί ἑ κατακτείνειε, Διὸς δ’ ἀλίτηται ἐφετμάς.
sentences.tr:
mē ho men achnymenēi kradiēi cholon ouk erysaito
paida idōn, Achilēï d’ orintheiē philon ētor,
kai he katakteineie, Dios d’ alitētai ephetmas.
sentences.l:
lest he, with grieving heart, his anger not hold back
on seeing his child, and in Achilles be stirred his dear heart,
and he kill him, and offend against the commands of Zeus.
sentences.i: lest Priam, grieving at heart, should fail to hold back his anger at the sight of his son, and Achilles’ heart be stirred, and he kill him and offend against the commands of Zeus.
sentences.n: μή begins a fear clause that runs to the end of 586. ὃ μέν ‘he’ is Priam, set against Ἀχιλῆϊ in the second clause. ἀχνυμένῃ κραδίῃ is ‘with grieving heart’ (dative of manner), and οὐκ ἐρύσαιτο is ‘would not hold back’ his anger (χόλον), the aorist optative middle of ἐρύομαι, which elsewhere is ‘protect, draw’; here the anger is the thing drawn in and kept back. παῖδα ἰδών ‘on seeing his child’. Ἀχιλῆϊ δ’ ὀρινθείη φίλον ἦτορ is ‘and his dear heart be stirred in Achilles’ (ὀρίνω ‘stir’, an aorist passive optative); ἑ is ‘him’, the object of κατακτείνειε ‘he might kill’. The last verb, ἀλίτηται, is the aorist subjunctive of ἀλιτραίνω ‘offend against’, the mood changing from the optatives; Διὸς … ἐφετμάς ‘the commands of Zeus’.

sentences.t:
τὸν δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν δμῳαὶ λοῦσαν καὶ χρῖσαν ἐλαίῳ,
ἀμφὶ δέ μιν φᾶρος καλὸν βάλον ἠδὲ χιτῶνα,
αὐτὸς τόν γ’ Ἀχιλεὺς λεχέων ἐπέθηκεν ἀείρας,
σὺν δ’ ἕταροι ἤειραν ἐϋξέστην ἐπ’ ἀπήνην.
sentences.tr:
ton d’ epei oun dmōiai lousan kai chrisan elaiōi,
amphi de min pharos kalon balon ēde chitōna,
autos ton g’ Achileus lecheōn epethēken aeiras,
syn d’ hetaroi ēeiran eÿxestēn ep’ apēnēn.
sentences.l:
And him when then the maidservants had washed and anointed with oil,
and about him a fine cloak had thrown, and a tunic,
himself, Achilles, onto a bedstead put him, having lifted him,
and with him his companions lifted him onto the well-polished wagon.
sentences.i: And when the maids had washed him and anointed him with oil, and had thrown a fine cloak and a tunic about him, Achilles himself lifted him and laid him on a bier, and his companions with him lifted him up onto the well-polished wagon.
sentences.n: The first two lines are formulaic: the first stands also in the Odyssey, and the second there has χλαῖναν ‘cloak’ where this has φᾶρος, the singular of φάρεα at 580 (‘cloak’ again). τὸν δ’ ‘him’ is Hector; δμῳαί are the ‘maidservants’ of 582, λοῦσαν and χρῖσαν the aorists of λούω ‘wash’ and χρίω ‘anoint’; ἀμφί … βάλον ‘threw about’ has ἀμφί parted from its verb. αὐτὸς … Ἀχιλεύς ‘Achilles himself’ is the one who lifts the body (ἀείρας) and lays it on λεχέων, a genitive after ἐπέθηκεν ‘put on’: λέχος is ‘bed’, here the bier. σὺν δ’ ἕταροι ἤειραν is ‘and with him the companions lifted’ (ἤειραν the aorist of ἀείρω), the object, the body on its bier, being understood; ἐϋξέστην ‘well-polished’ agrees with ἀπήνην ‘wagon’.

sentences.t: ᾤμωξέν τ’ ἄρ’ ἔπειτα, φίλον δ’ ὀνόμηνεν ἑταῖρον·
sentences.tr: ōimōxen t’ ar’ epeita, philon d’ onomēnen hetairon·
sentences.l: And he cried out then, and called by name his dear companion:
sentences.i: Then he cried out and called his dear companion by name:
sentences.n: ᾤμωξεν is ‘he cried out’ (οἰμώζω), and φίλον … ἑταῖρον ‘his dear companion’ is the dead Patroclus, called by name (ὀνόμηνεν, aorist of ὀνομαίνω); the speech to him follows. The line is shared with 23.178, where Achilles also speaks to Patroclus.

sentences.t:
μή μοι Πάτροκλε σκυδμαινέμεν, αἴ κε πύθηαι
εἰν Ἄϊδός περ ἐὼν ὅτι Ἕκτορα δῖον ἔλυσα
πατρὶ φίλῳ, ἐπεὶ οὔ μοι ἀεικέα δῶκεν ἄποινα.
sentences.tr:
mē moi Patrokle skydmainemen, ai ke pythēai
ein Aïdos per eōn hoti Hektora dion elysa
patri philōi, epei ou moi aeikea dōken apoina.
sentences.l:
“Do not, Patroclus, be indignant at me, if you learn,
even in Hades being, that heavenly Hector I released
to his dear father, since he gave me not unseemly ransom.
sentences.i: “Do not be indignant with me, Patroclus, if you learn, even in the house of Hades, that I released heavenly Hector to his dear father; for the ransom he gave me was not unseemly.
sentences.n: μή μοι … σκυδμαινέμεν is an infinitive used as an imperative, ‘do not be indignant at me’ (σκυδμαίνω ‘be indignant, take offence’). αἴ κε πύθηαι is ‘if you learn’ (aorist subjunctive of πυνθάνομαι). εἰν Ἄϊδός περ ἐών is ‘even though you are in Hades’, εἰν being ἐν and the genitive Ἄϊδος having ‘house’ understood. Ἕκτορα δῖον is ‘heavenly Hector’, ἔλυσα ‘I released’, πατρὶ φίλῳ ‘to his dear father’. ἐπεὶ οὔ μοι ἀεικέα δῶκεν ἄποινα is ‘since he gave me not unseemly ransom’, a double negative that means a fitting ransom; ἀεικέα (ἀεικής ‘unseemly’) agrees with ἄποινα.

sentences.t: σοὶ δ’ αὖ ἐγὼ καὶ τῶνδ’ ἀποδάσσομαι ὅσσ’ ἐπέοικεν.
sentences.tr: soi d’ au egō kai tōnd’ apodassomai hoss’ epeoiken.
sentences.l: and to you in turn I too of these shall apportion as much as is fitting.”
sentences.i: and to you in turn I will give a share of these things too, as much as is fitting.”
sentences.n: σοὶ δ’ αὖ is ‘and to you in turn’; ἐγώ ‘I’ and καί ‘also’; τῶνδ’ ‘of these’ is a partitive genitive, the ransom. ἀποδάσσομαι is the future middle of ἀποδατέομαι ‘portion out, give a share’; ὅσσ’ ἐπέοικεν is ‘as much as befits’ (ἐπέοικε, the perfect of ἐπί + ἔοικα, ‘it is fitting’, with present sense). The closing mark ends Achilles’ speech; the next part opens after it.
